\begin{abstract}
\iffalse
  A clear and well-documented \LaTeX\ document is presented as an
  article formatted for publication by ACM in a conference proceedings
  or journal publication. Based on the ``acmart'' document class, this
  article presents and explains many of the common variations, as well
  as many of the formatting elements an author may use in the
  preparation of the documentation of their work.
\fi
Deep Hedging learns sequential hedging policies directly from market states,
transaction costs, and a risk-sensitive objective, but its neural decisions
are difficult to audit. ProtoHedge addresses this problem by routing each
hedge through a finite set of representative market states, or prototypes:
the action is determined by the current state's similarity to those
prototypes and their associated hedge responses. This paper tests whether that
interpretability mechanism remains viable on historical option data, where
market regimes, frictions, and non-stationarity matter. We compare ProtoHedge
with classical delta-style rules and a matched black-box Deep Hedging benchmark
under common costs, bounds, accounting, and model-selection controls. In the
European short-call panel, ProtoHedge produces the strongest mean and tail
frontiers while using less position-bound occupancy on average. Prototype use
is concentrated, regime-sensitive, and traceable to concrete historical
episodes, supporting the claim that interpretability can be added to deep
hedging without sacrificing empirical competitiveness.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Deep hedging replaces a prescribed analytical hedge with a policy learned
from market states, realized trading costs, and a risk-sensitive objective.
This flexibility is valuable when hedging is discrete, costly, constrained,
and exposed to dynamics that depart from a stylized pricing model. Its
central practical weakness is that a neural policy can be difficult to
audit: strong performance alone does not explain which market states drive a
hedge, whether comparable states receive comparable actions, or whether a
model has learned a stable economic rule.

ProtoHedge addresses this problem by routing each decision through a finite
set of representative market states, called prototypes. The original paper
established that this prototype structure can retain much of the performance
of an unrestricted neural hedge in Black--Scholes and stochastic-volatility
simulations. The unresolved question is empirical. Historical options data
contain non-stationarity, imperfect liquidity, changing volatility, and
discontinuous episodes that cannot be fully captured by a controlled
simulator.

This paper evaluates ProtoHedge on historical U.S.\ option-hedging episodes.
Our contribution is empirical rather than architectural: we preserve the
fixed-prototype design and test whether its performance--interpretability
tradeoff survives on real market data. The paper makes four contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We construct a ten-ticker panel of 30,797 contiguous 20-step
    historical option-hedging episodes from WRDS-sourced underlying and option
    data.
    \item We evaluate ProtoHedge against unhedged exposure, transparent
    delta-style rules, and a matched black-box Deep Hedging benchmark under
    transaction costs, hard bounds, step-wise accounting, and multi-seed
    validation-based selection.
    \item We show that ProtoHedge is competitive across the panel while
    reducing average reliance on hard position bounds.
    \item We test interpretability directly through prototype concentration,
    regime-dependent usage, and retrieval of nearest historical episodes.
\end{enumerate}









\section{ProtoHedge and the Empirical Validation Problem}
\label{sec:protohedge_empirical_problem}

\subsection{Deep Hedging as Sequential Risk Management}
\label{subsec:deep_hedging_background}

Deep hedging replaces a prescribed replication formula with a policy learned
from observed market states and a risk-sensitive hedging objective. Let
$P_t \in \mathbb{R}^m$ be the vector of hedge-instrument prices, let $h_t$ be
the cumulative hedge inventory, and let $\tau_t$ denote time remaining. At
time $t$, a policy observes a state such as
\[
x_t = (P_t, h_{t-1}, \tau_t)
\]
and outputs a trade increment
\[
a_t = \pi_\theta(x_t), \qquad
h_t = \Pi_{\mathcal{H}}(h_{t-1}+a_t),
\]
where $\Pi_{\mathcal{H}}$ enforces the admissible position set. For an option
payoff $H(P_{0:T})$ and per-unit transaction-cost vector $\kappa_t$, the
terminal gain can be written schematically as
\[
G^{\pi_\theta}
=
-H(P_{0:T})
+
\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} h_t^\top(P_{t+1}-P_t)
-
\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\kappa_t^\top |a_t|.
\]
The agent is trained to optimize a risk criterion, for example
\[
\min_\theta \operatorname{CVaR}_{\alpha}\!\left(-G^{\pi_\theta}\right),
\]
rather than to reproduce a model-implied delta exactly. This formulation
accommodates discrete rebalancing, costs, hard bounds, and dynamics that need
not follow a stylized pricing model.

A standard, or black-box, Deep Hedging policy represents $\pi_\theta$ by a
feed-forward neural network. It is a necessary performance benchmark in this
paper because it has the same information, objective, costs, and constraints
as ProtoHedge. Its limitation is diagnostic rather than computational: an
action can be evaluated without revealing which market states motivated it or
whether the policy has learned an economically stable rule.

\subsection{ProtoHedge: Fixed Prototypes as an Interpretable Policy}
\label{subsec:protohedge_background}

ProtoHedge retains the deep-hedging objective but restricts action generation
to a finite collection of representative states
\[
\mathcal{P}=\{p_1,\ldots,p_K\}.
\]
In the fixed-prototype design studied here, each $p_k$ is an observed
standardized state selected from the empirical state distribution. For a
standardized current state $\tilde{x}_t$, nonnegative feature weights
$\gamma$, and a shared learned projection $f_\phi$, ProtoHedge forms
\[
z_t=f_\phi(\gamma\odot\tilde{x}_t), \qquad
z_k^{p}=f_\phi(\gamma\odot p_k),
\]
then measures squared distances and converts them into normalized prototype
weights:
\[
d_{t,k}=\lVert z_t-z_k^{p}\rVert_2^2,
\qquad
\alpha_{t,k}
=
\frac{\exp(-d_{t,k})}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(-d_{t,j})}.
\]
Each prototype has an associated trainable, bounded hedge response
$b_k\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$. The action is the similarity-weighted combination
\[
a_t=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_{t,k}b_k.
\]

This decomposition is the central ProtoHedge mechanism. For every hedge
decision, the model exposes the prototypes with the largest weights, their
representative market states, and their associated actions. A reviewer can
therefore trace a decision to examples of historically observed states rather
than only to opaque network parameters. Concentrated use of a small subset of
prototypes, systematic shifts in $\alpha_{t,k}$ across regimes, and retrieval
of the nearest historical episodes provide direct, testable forms of
interpretability.

The anchors $p_k$ remain fixed during training in the present study; the
projection $f_\phi$ and the prototype actions $b_k$ are learned. This
preserves the original ProtoHedge premise that a prototype should remain tied
to an actual representative state, rather than drifting to an uninterpretable
parameter value. Section~\ref{sec:experimental_framework} specifies how the
prototypes are extracted, how $K$ and similarity weighting are varied, and how
the policy is trained.

\subsection{Why the Empirical Test Matters}
\label{subsec:empirical_gap}

The original ProtoHedge study showed that prototype-based policies can remain
competitive in Black--Scholes and stochastic-volatility simulations. Historical
option data pose a materially different test: volatility and liquidity vary
over time, option observations are noisy, trading is costly and constrained,
and market paths contain regime shifts and discontinuities. The
interpretability claim is also stronger on real data, because a useful
prototype should correspond to a recognizable historical state rather than
only to a simulator-generated configuration.

Accordingly, this paper evaluates whether ProtoHedge remains competitive with
matched black-box Deep Hedging and transparent delta-style baselines while
avoiding excessive reliance on hard position bounds. It also tests whether
prototype use is concentrated, regime-dependent, and retrievable as concrete
historical episodes. We conduct this evaluation for both terminal European
short calls and path-dependent Asian short calls, allowing the
performance--interpretability tradeoff to be assessed under two economically
distinct liabilities.












\section{Experimental Framework}
\label{sec:experimental_framework}

This section describes the empirical design used to evaluate ProtoHedge on historical market data. Our implementation is deliberately conservative. We use fixed-length out-of-sample hedging episodes, explicit transaction costs, bounded trading actions, bounded cumulative hedge positions, validation-based model selection, and multi-seed evaluation. The goal is not merely to train a profitable hedge in sample, but to assess whether ProtoHedge remains competitive with vanilla Deep Hedging under a realistic and reproducible real-data protocol.

\subsection{Data and Episode Construction}
\label{subsec:data_episode_construction}

Our real-data experiments are based on historical U.S. equity and ETF option data obtained through WRDS, combining underlying spot-price histories with daily listed option records. The final panel contains ten liquid underlyings spanning broad equity indices, sector ETFs, fixed income, and single-name equities:
\[
\{\texttt{AAPL}, \texttt{IWM}, \texttt{NVDA}, \texttt{QQQ}, \texttt{SPY}, \texttt{TLT}, \texttt{XLE}, \texttt{XLF}, \texttt{XLK}, \texttt{XLV}\}.
\]
For each ticker, the cleaned feature panel runs from 2005-01-11 to 2024-12-31.

The raw option-chain data are filtered to call options and aligned with the corresponding daily spot series. For each date, we select a single liquid near-at-the-money call contract by sorting candidate options according to:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item absolute distance between strike and spot,
    \item absolute distance between the contract's days-to-expiration and a 30-day target maturity,
    \item bid--ask spread,
    \item open interest (descending), and
    \item volume (descending),
\end{enumerate}
subject to a maturity filter of 20 to 40 calendar days to expiration. This yields a daily panel of one representative short-dated near-ATM call per underlying.

The resulting per-date feature vector is
\[
x_t^{\mathrm{raw}} = \bigl(S_t,\; C_t,\; \Delta^{\mathrm{call}}_t,\; \nu_t,\; \sigma^{\mathrm{impl}}_t \bigr),
\]
where $S_t$ is the underlying spot, $C_t$ is the selected call price, $\Delta^{\mathrm{call}}_t$ is the selected call delta, $\nu_t$ is the selected call vega, and $\sigma^{\mathrm{impl}}_t$ is implied volatility. These features are stored in the episode tensor in the fixed order
\[
(\texttt{spot},\; \texttt{call\_price},\; \texttt{call\_delta},\; \texttt{call\_vega},\; \texttt{ivol}).
\]

Historical hedging episodes are constructed as rolling 20-step windows. Importantly, windows are created only within contiguous trading-date blocks: whenever the gap between consecutive observation dates exceeds four calendar days, a new block is started. This prevents the episode builder from stitching together disjoint option cycles separated by large holes in the cleaned panel. Letting $\tau=20$ denote the episode length, each final sample is a tensor in
\[
\mathbb{R}^{\tau \times 5}.
\]
Across the ten-ticker panel, this procedure yields 30{,}797 usable 20-step episodes in total.

Although the raw episode tensor contains five market features, the learning models do not consume all five directly. The hedging agents are trained on the state representation used by the deep hedging gym, namely current hedgeable prices, current hedge inventory, and time remaining. Concretely, the learned policies use the feature list
\[
(\texttt{price},\; \texttt{delta},\; \texttt{time\_left}),
\]
where \texttt{price} is the two-dimensional vector of current spot and current selected call price, \texttt{delta} denotes the current cumulative hedge position in the two traded instruments, and \texttt{time\_left} is the remaining time to maturity. The richer market panel remains important because it defines the liability, the classical baselines, the transaction-cost model, and the regime-analysis variables.

Finally, for numerical stability and cross-path comparability, the real-data world normalizes spot, call price, and call vega by each path's initial spot level. Under this normalization, a liability struck at-the-money at inception has normalized strike one, while remaining equivalent to a strike of $S_0$ in raw price units.

\subsection{Hedging Tasks}
\label{subsec:hedging_tasks}

We study two liabilities on the same historical episode panel.

\paragraph{European ATM short call.}
The primary task is to hedge a short at-the-money European call over a 20-step historical episode. If $S_{i,0}$ denotes the initial spot on episode $i$, then the strike is set to
\[
K_i = S_{i,0}.
\]
The liability payoff at maturity is
\[
H_i^{\mathrm{Euro}} = -\max(S_{i,T} - K_i, 0),
\]
where the negative sign reflects the fact that the hedger is short the option.

\paragraph{Asian ATM short call.}
The path-dependent extension replaces the European liability with an arithmetic-average Asian call, again struck at-the-money at episode start:
\[
K_i = S_{i,0}.
\]
Let the episode contain $T$ trading decisions. The Asian liability is
\[
H_i^{\mathrm{Asian}} = -\max\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} S_{i,t} - K_i,\, 0\right).
\]
In the implementation used for the final paper sweep, the averaging window spans the full historical episode.

\paragraph{Hedge instruments and actions.}
The hedge may trade in two liquid instruments:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the underlying spot instrument, and
    \item the selected near-ATM listed call option.
\end{enumerate}
The action at each step is therefore two-dimensional,
\[
a_t = \bigl(a_t^{(S)}, a_t^{(C)}\bigr),
\]
where each component denotes a trade increment rather than an absolute target position. The cumulative hedge inventory evolves recursively as
\[
\delta_t = \delta_{t-1} + a_t.
\]

\paragraph{Step-wise hedge accounting.}
All reported experiments use step-wise hedge accounting rather than a terminal shortcut. If $\Delta S_t$ and $\Delta C_t$ denote the next-step changes in the spot and option hedge instruments, then the pathwise hedge P\&L is accumulated as
\[
\mathrm{PnL}_i = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left(a_{i,t}^{(S)} \Delta S_{i,t} + a_{i,t}^{(C)} \Delta C_{i,t}\right).
\]
This choice is important empirically. In earlier exploratory real-data runs, more permissive accounting and looser constraints could produce apparently strong results together with unrealistic cumulative-bound saturation. The current step-wise setup is intentionally stricter and better aligned with the actual sequence of hedge rebalancing decisions.

\paragraph{Transaction costs.}
Trading costs are imposed separately on spot and option trades. The per-unit spot trading-cost coefficient is
\[
c_{i,t}^{(S)} = 0.0002\,|S_{i,t}|.
\]
The per-unit option trading-cost coefficient is
\[
c_{i,t}^{(C)} = 0.02\,|\nu_{i,t}| + 0.0002\,|\Delta^{\mathrm{call}}_{i,t}| + 0.0005\,|C_{i,t}|.
\]
The realized trading cost on episode $i$ is therefore
\[
\mathrm{Cost}_i
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\left(
|a_{i,t}^{(S)}|\,c_{i,t}^{(S)}
+
|a_{i,t}^{(C)}|\,c_{i,t}^{(C)}
\right).
\]

\paragraph{Gains.}
For both liabilities, the terminal hedging gain is defined as
\[
G_i = H_i + \mathrm{PnL}_i - \mathrm{Cost}_i.
\]
This is the central outcome used throughout the empirical evaluation.

\subsection{Models and Baselines}
\label{subsec:models_baselines}

We compare ProtoHedge against both classical baselines and a black-box neural benchmark.

\paragraph{Unhedged.}
This baseline takes no hedge action:
\[
a_t \equiv 0.
\]
Its gain is simply the liability payoff.

\paragraph{Spot-Delta.}
This is a rule-based baseline that hedges only with the underlying spot instrument. At each step, the target cumulative spot position is set equal to the observed delta of the selected near-ATM call. The option hedge position remains zero. This baseline uses the market-provided option delta directly and therefore provides a transparent classical reference point.

\paragraph{Spot-Delta Band.}
This baseline extends Spot-Delta with a no-trade band. Instead of rebalancing to the point target at every step, the current cumulative spot position is left unchanged as long as it remains within
\[
[\Delta^{\mathrm{call}}_t - b,\; \Delta^{\mathrm{call}}_t + b],
\]
where $b \ge 0$ is a band width. If the current position exits the band, it is projected back to the closest boundary. We tune $b$ on the validation set using the grid
\[
b \in \{0.00,\;0.01,\;0.02,\;0.05,\;0.10,\;0.15\},
\]
selecting the band that maximizes validation mean gains.

\paragraph{Vanilla Deep Hedging.}
The main black-box benchmark is a feed-forward neural hedging policy trained end-to-end under the same world, friction model, and objective as ProtoHedge. The vanilla agent uses the state representation
\[
(\texttt{price},\; \texttt{delta},\; \texttt{time\_left}),
\]
and outputs a two-dimensional trade increment. In the reported panel runs, the vanilla network has width 20, depth 3, and Softplus activations.

\paragraph{ProtoHedge.}
ProtoHedge uses the same state representation and output space as vanilla Deep Hedging, but constrains action generation through a prototype layer. Each current state is compared to a finite collection of stored prototypes, and the resulting similarity pattern determines the hedge action. In the reported full grid, we vary:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the number of prototypes
    \[
    K \in \{10, 25, 50, 100\},
    \]
    \item the prototype source policy, using either a trained vanilla hedge or the Spot-Delta baseline as the source from which prototypes are extracted, and
    \item whether similarity is weighted or unweighted.
\end{enumerate}

Prototype extraction follows the same reusable pipeline throughout the repo. For a given source policy, we:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item construct the flattened feature matrix seen by the policy,
    \item standardize it with a \texttt{StandardScaler},
    \item apply $K$-means clustering in standardized feature space, and
    \item store, for each cluster, the nearest real standardized feature vector rather than the raw cluster centroid.
\end{enumerate}
This last step matters because it keeps each stored prototype tied to an actually observed market state rather than to an abstract average point with no direct empirical counterpart.

In the reported real-data panel runs, learned distance-feature weights are held fixed, i.e.\ we do not yet let prototypes or feature-weight vectors move during training. This keeps the present paper focused on empirical validation of the original fixed-prototype design.

\subsection{Training and Model Selection Protocol}
\label{subsec:training_protocol}

All real-data neural models are trained under the same multi-seed protocol.

\paragraph{Train/validation/test splits.}
For each ticker and each random seed, the episode tensor is randomly permuted at the path level and split into
\[
70\% \text{ train}, \qquad 15\% \text{ validation}, \qquad 15\% \text{ test}.
\]
The main reported panel uses the three seeds
\[
(1234,\;2345,\;3456).
\]

\paragraph{Optimization.}
All neural models are trained for 800 epochs using the same CVaR-based deep hedging objective with risk-aversion parameter one. The optimizer uses learning rate
\[
10^{-3},
\]
together with clipping safeguards already built into the training pipeline. Classical baselines are not trained in the neural sense, but they are evaluated on exactly the same splits and under the same friction model.

\paragraph{Feature normalization and state semantics.}
The real-data world is run in normalized mode. Spot, call price, and call vega are divided pathwise by the initial spot, while the state passed to the learning agent at each step consists of current hedgeable prices, current hedge inventory, and time remaining. This keeps the neural state compact and comparable across underlyings while preserving the original market information needed for payoff definition, baseline construction, and regime analysis.

\paragraph{Validation-based checkpoint selection.}
Model selection is based on the validation split, not on the training loss alone. Let $L_{\mathrm{val}}$ denote the validation objective. For the final robust panel runs, checkpoints are ranked by the selection score
\[
\mathcal{S}
=
L_{\mathrm{val}}
+
\alpha_a \,\overline{|a|}
+
\alpha_\delta \,\overline{|\delta|}
+
\alpha_b \,\mathrm{BO}
+
\alpha_p \,\mathrm{PT},
\]
where $\overline{|a|}$ is mean absolute action magnitude on the validation set, $\overline{|\delta|}$ is mean absolute cumulative position magnitude, $\mathrm{BO}$ is validation bound occupancy, and $\mathrm{PT}$ is the fraction of validation paths that touch any cumulative bound. In the reported full runs, we use
\[
\alpha_a = 0.005,\qquad
\alpha_\delta = 0.010,\qquad
\alpha_b = 0.100,\qquad
\alpha_p = 0.
\]
Thus, validation selection explicitly favors models that do not rely excessively on large actions, large cumulative positions, or persistent boundary saturation.

\paragraph{Regularization.}
In addition to validation-time selection penalties, the training loss includes mild regularization terms on action and cumulative-position magnitude:
\[
\lambda_a = 0.001,
\qquad
\lambda_\delta = 0.002.
\]
Concretely, if $L_{\mathrm{hedge}}$ is the base objective, then the optimized loss is
\[
L_{\mathrm{train}}
=
L_{\mathrm{hedge}}
+
\lambda_a \,\mathbb{E}[|a|]
+
\lambda_\delta \,\mathbb{E}[|\delta|].
\]
These penalties are deliberately mild: they do not dominate the objective, but they discourage the model from achieving performance through unnecessarily aggressive trading.

\paragraph{Trade bounds and cumulative position bounds.}
The final reported real-data runs impose both action-level and cumulative-position bounds. At every step and for each traded instrument, trade increments are clipped to
\[
[-1,\,1],
\]
and cumulative hedge positions are also constrained to
\[
[-1,\,1].
\]
These bounds are scientifically important. In exploratory unconstrained runs, apparent performance improvements could be accompanied by heavy saturation at the position boundaries. The bounded protocol is designed to test whether ProtoHedge remains competitive without relying on unrealistic edge-of-feasible-region behavior.

\paragraph{Paper sweep design.}
For the European-call panel, the final full sweep evaluates the full ProtoHedge grid described above across all ten tickers and all three seeds. The Asian-call extension uses the same empirical framework and, in the final notebook implementation, can be run with the same grid and the same seed schedule. This allows direct comparison between terminal and path-dependent liabilities without changing the training pipeline.

\subsection{Evaluation Metrics}
\label{subsec:evaluation_metrics}

We evaluate models at both the hedging-performance level and the interpretability level.

\paragraph{Primary performance metrics.}
For each fitted model and each test split, we compute:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item mean gains,
    \[
    \mathbb{E}[G],
    \]
    \item the empirical 5\% Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk of gains,
    \[
    \mathrm{VaR}_{5\%}(G), \qquad \mathrm{CVaR}_{5\%}(G),
    \]
    \item shortfall probability,
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(G<0),
    \]
    and
    \item realized mean trading-cost and hedge-P\&L summaries.
\end{enumerate}
In the paper narrative, mean gains and $\mathrm{CVaR}_{5\%}$ are the headline performance measures. Shortfall probability is retained as a secondary summary rather than the sole criterion of success.

\paragraph{Position-bound diagnostics.}
Because constrained hedging behavior is a central part of the empirical question, we also record:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the fraction of all path--step--instrument positions lying at either cumulative position bound,
    \item the fraction lying specifically at the upper or lower bound, and
    \item the fraction of paths that touch any cumulative position bound at least once.
\end{enumerate}
We refer to the first quantity as \emph{bound occupancy}. Lower bound occupancy is interpreted as evidence that a model is operating more consistently in the interior of the feasible region, which is economically preferable all else equal.

\paragraph{Robust-screen criterion.}
When constructing paper frontiers among ProtoHedge models, we apply a robustness screen based on average bound occupancy and path-touch behavior. In the final reported panel setup, models with excessive bound saturation are excluded from the empirical frontier even if they perform well on raw mean gains. This prevents the final comparison from being driven by unrealistic edge-seeking solutions.

\paragraph{Prototype concentration metrics.}
For ProtoHedge models, we further compute:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item average prototype weight across all paths and time steps,
    \item top-1 prototype frequency, i.e.\ the proportion of decisions for which each prototype receives the highest weight, and
    \item cumulative usage mass of the top-$k$ prototypes.
\end{enumerate}
These metrics quantify whether decisions are routed through a small number of dominant prototype states or diffusely across many prototypes.

\paragraph{Regime-sensitive interpretability metrics.}
To test whether prototype use changes systematically with market conditions, we form episode-level regime labels from the historical paths:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{return regime}, using terciles of terminal return,
    \item \emph{volatility regime}, using terciles of average implied volatility, and
    \item \emph{drawdown regime}, using terciles of maximum realized drawdown.
\end{itemize}
This yields labels of the form
\[
\{\text{down},\text{middle},\text{up}\},\quad
\{\text{low\_vol},\text{mid\_vol},\text{high\_vol}\},\quad
\{\text{mild\_dd},\text{mid\_dd},\text{deep\_dd}\}.
\]
Within each regime, we summarize gains, tail risk, shortfall, and average prototype weights. This lets us test whether the same few prototypes dominate everywhere, or whether ProtoHedge reallocates attention across market states in a regime-sensitive way.

\paragraph{Nearest historical states.}
Finally, for the dominant prototypes, we recover the nearest historical feature vectors and corresponding underlying paths. This allows us to move beyond abstract prototype coordinates and ask whether the most-used prototypes correspond to recognizable empirical market scenarios. This step is central to the interpretability claim of the paper: the prototype mechanism is not merely sparse, but empirically inspectable.









\section{Real-Data Empirical Results}
\label{sec:empirical_results}

This section evaluates whether ProtoHedge preserves a favorable
performance--interpretability tradeoff on historical option-hedging
episodes. All reported European-option results use the common protocol
described in Section~\ref{sec:experimental_framework}: three random
seeds, held-out test episodes, step-wise hedge accounting, transaction
costs, hard trade and cumulative-position bounds, and validation-based
checkpoint selection. For each ticker, results are first averaged over
seeds and then aggregated with equal weight across the ten tickers.

\subsection{European-Option Panel Results}

Table~\ref{tab:european-panel-average} reports the main panel-level
comparison. The mean-oriented ProtoHedge frontier achieves the best
average mean gains across the ten-ticker panel, while the tail-oriented
ProtoHedge frontier achieves the best average empirical
CVaR$_{5\%}$. The result is therefore not that one ProtoHedge
configuration dominates every criterion. Rather, the prototype model
produces an interpretable mean--tail frontier that is at least as
competitive as vanilla Deep Hedging under both objectives.

All models face the same short-call liability, transaction-cost model,
and position constraints. Thus, the relative comparison is the central
object of interest. The negative level of average gains reflects the
conservative constrained evaluation environment and should not be
interpreted as evidence that the ordering among hedges is uninformative.
Under this common protocol, a less negative gain or CVaR value is better.

\subsection{Position-Bound Analysis}

Position bounds prevent a learned hedge from taking unrealistically
large cumulative exposures. Bound occupancy therefore measures how
often a policy is effectively pressed against the edge of the feasible
trading region. A policy with strong performance but persistent
bound-saturation is less economically credible, because its apparent
performance may depend heavily on the imposed constraint rather than on
a stable hedge rule.

The aggregate evidence favors ProtoHedge. Vanilla Deep Hedging has mean
bound occupancy of $0.0775$, compared with $0.0486$ for the
mean-oriented ProtoHedge frontier and $0.0304$ for the tail-oriented
frontier. These correspond to average reductions of approximately
$37\%$ and $61\%$, respectively, relative to vanilla. The improvement
is not universal: for TLT, XLE, XLF, and XLV, the selected tail frontier
has higher occupancy than vanilla. This heterogeneity is important and
shows why the paper reports per-ticker diagnostics rather than only a
pooled average.

Figure~\ref{fig:european-bound-heatmap} makes this diagnostic
transparent. The learned-model columns should be compared within each
row; darker or larger values correspond to more frequent contact with a
hard cumulative-position limit. ProtoHedge often achieves competitive
mean or tail performance without greater bound reliance, particularly
for AAPL, IWM, NVDA, QQQ, and SPY.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{../paper/final_notebook_assets/real_data_panel/panel_bound_heatmap.png}
\caption{Cumulative position-bound occupancy by ticker and model.
Each cell is the fraction of held-out decision times at which the
cumulative hedge is at a hard position limit. Lower values are more
economically credible. The comparison among learned policies shows that
ProtoHedge often reduces reliance on the hard bounds relative to vanilla
Deep Hedging.}
\Description{Heatmap of cumulative position-bound occupancy for six
model families across ten tickers.}
\label{fig:european-bound-heatmap}
\end{figure*}

The bound analysis strengthens the main performance result. ProtoHedge
does not obtain its favorable panel-level mean and CVaR performance by
systematically taking more extreme feasible positions. Instead, the
prototype bottleneck is consistent with a less boundary-driven policy
on average, while preserving competitive hedging outcomes.

\subsection{Interpretability Verification}

Performance alone does not establish that ProtoHedge is interpretable.
We therefore inspect the learned prototype mechanism directly using a
representative QQQ frontier model with $25$ prototypes. The goal is not
to claim that a small number of states completely explains every
decision, but to test whether the policy actually routes decisions
through a sparse and inspectable set of recurring empirical states.

Figure~\ref{fig:qqq-prototype-concentration} reports cumulative
prototype usage after sorting prototypes from most to least used. The
three most-used prototypes account for $58.4\%$ of total assignment
mass, and the ten most-used prototypes account for approximately
$99.6\%$. Thus, although the model is supplied with 25 prototypes, its
decisions are effectively concentrated in a much smaller subset of
recurrently used state representatives.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{../paper/final_notebook_assets/real_data_panel/qqq_prototype_concentration.png}
\caption{Prototype concentration for a representative QQQ ProtoHedge
model with 25 prototypes. The horizontal axis gives the number of
most-used prototypes retained, and the vertical axis gives their
cumulative assignment mass. The steep initial increase shows that a
small subset of prototypes explains most decisions.}
\Description{Cumulative prototype-usage curve for the representative QQQ
ProtoHedge model.}
\label{fig:qqq-prototype-concentration}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:qqq-volatility-usage} tests whether this usage is
state-dependent rather than static. Each row is a volatility regime and
each column is a prototype; color denotes the average similarity weight
assigned in that regime. Several dominant prototypes change
substantially across regimes. For example, prototype 8 is most prominent
in low-volatility episodes, whereas prototypes 18 and 23 receive
substantially more weight in high-volatility episodes. This behavior is
consistent with the intended interpretation of ProtoHedge: distinct
representative states become relevant under different market
conditions.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{../paper/final_notebook_assets/real_data_panel/qqq_vol_regime_prototype_usage.png}
\caption{Prototype usage by realized-volatility regime for the
representative QQQ model. Rows correspond to low-, medium-, and
high-volatility held-out episodes; columns correspond to individual
prototypes; color represents average prototype-assignment weight.
Regime-specific changes in the dominant columns show that the prototype
layer responds to market conditions rather than applying a fixed
mixture of prototypes.}
\Description{Heatmap of prototype-assignment weights across volatility
regimes for the representative QQQ ProtoHedge model.}
\label{fig:qqq-volatility-usage}
\end{figure*}

Finally, Figure~\ref{fig:qqq-nearest-episodes} grounds the dominant
prototypes in actual historical episodes. Each panel shows the
normalized spot path nearest to one of the most-used prototypes, and
the dashed vertical line marks the time step at which the prototype
match occurs. The retrieved examples are recognizable market
configurations---including moderately rising, recovering, and sharply
drawn-down paths---rather than abstract latent coordinates. This
retrieval property is the practical interpretability advantage of
ProtoHedge: a hedge decision can be linked back to concrete historical
situations that a domain expert can inspect.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{../paper/final_notebook_assets/real_data_panel/qqq_nearest_historical_episodes.png}
\caption{Nearest historical QQQ episodes for four dominant prototypes.
Each subplot shows a normalized 20-step spot path; the dashed line marks
the state that is nearest to the corresponding prototype. These
retrievals connect the learned prototype representation to concrete
historical market trajectories.}
\Description{Four normalized historical QQQ paths nearest to dominant
prototypes, with dashed lines marking the matched decision times.}
\label{fig:qqq-nearest-episodes}
\end{figure*}

Together, the concentration, regime-usage, and nearest-episode
diagnostics provide direct evidence that the prototype layer is active
and inspectable in the real-data setting. They do not prove that every
prototype has a unique economic interpretation, but they rule out the
simpler concern that prototypes are merely decorative parameters with
diffuse or state-invariant usage.

\subsection{Asian-Option Results}

The final empirical extension applies the same framework to an
at-the-money short Asian call. Unlike the European liability, the Asian
payoff depends on the arithmetic average of the underlying over the
specified averaging window. This experiment therefore tests whether
ProtoHedge remains competitive when the liability depends on the path
rather than solely on the terminal underlying price.

The Asian-option panel will use the same ten tickers, episode
construction, train--validation--test splits, three-seed protocol,
transaction costs, position constraints, model grid, and
interpretability diagnostics as the European experiment. The analysis
will answer two questions:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item Does ProtoHedge remain competitive with vanilla Deep Hedging
    and the delta baselines on mean gains and CVaR$_{5\%}$ when hedging a
    path-dependent liability?
    \item Do the learned prototypes remain concentrated, regime-aware,
    and traceable to coherent historical paths when the payoff depends
    on path history?
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion and Limitations}
\label{sec:discussion}

The evidence in this paper supports the empirical-validation motivation
of ProtoHedge. On a ten-ticker panel of historical European-option
hedging episodes, ProtoHedge remains competitive with standard Deep
Hedging while retaining a directly inspectable prototype layer. The
mean-oriented ProtoHedge frontier achieves the strongest average mean
gains across the panel, while the tail-oriented frontier achieves the
strongest average empirical CVaR$_{5\%}$. Both ProtoHedge frontiers also
have lower average position-bound occupancy than standard Deep Hedging.

The appropriate interpretation is not that ProtoHedge universally
dominates all hedging methods. Rather, the results show that imposing a
prototype bottleneck need not cause a large empirical performance loss.
In the present setting, the bottleneck can coincide with slightly better
average gains or tail outcomes, while making the learned policy more
auditable. This is the central performance--interpretability tradeoff
that ProtoHedge was designed to deliver.

\subsection{Where ProtoHedge Works}

ProtoHedge performs particularly well on the criteria most closely
aligned with the paper's motivation. First, the mean-oriented frontier
improves on standard Deep Hedging in average mean gains for all ten
tickers. Second, the tail-oriented frontier improves empirical
CVaR$_{5\%}$ relative to standard Deep Hedging for all ten tickers.
These results span broad-market ETFs, sector ETFs, a Treasury ETF, and
large-cap individual equities, suggesting that the finding is not tied
to a single underlying.

The position-bound analysis provides a second positive result. On
average, both ProtoHedge frontiers spend less time at hard cumulative
position limits than standard Deep Hedging. This matters because a
policy that repeatedly sits at a constraint may derive apparent
performance from extreme feasible exposures rather than from a stable
hedging rule. The lower average bound occupancy of ProtoHedge therefore
strengthens, rather than weakens, the interpretation of its competitive
performance.

Finally, the prototype diagnostics show that the interpretability
mechanism remains active on real data. In the representative QQQ
analysis, most prototype usage mass is concentrated in a small subset
of the available prototypes, the dominant prototypes shift across
return, volatility, and drawdown regimes, and prototype matches can be
retrieved as concrete historical price paths. This does not mean that
every prototype has a single universal economic label. It does mean
that the policy can be examined through recurring market states instead
of only through opaque neural-network weights.

\subsection{Where ProtoHedge Does Not Dominate}

The results do not support a claim of universal superiority. The
relative advantage varies by ticker, metric, and selected frontier. For
example, the tail-oriented ProtoHedge frontier has higher bound
occupancy than standard Deep Hedging for several tickers, including TLT,
XLE, XLF, and XLV. Similarly, the simple unhedged and delta-style
baselines remain competitive on some secondary metrics, particularly
shortfall probability under the current gain definition.

This variation is economically plausible. Hedging performance depends
on the underlying's return distribution, implied-volatility behavior,
liquidity, option-market quality, and the interaction between
transaction costs and position constraints. ProtoHedge should
therefore be understood as an interpretable alternative with a
favorable average tradeoff, not as a replacement for every black-box or
classical hedge in every market.

The current results also do not establish that a single fixed
ProtoHedge configuration is optimal across all assets. The reported
mean and tail frontiers summarize screened configurations within each
ticker. A practitioner seeking to deploy one model specification across
markets would need an additional validation exercise that fixes the
architecture and hyperparameters before the final test evaluation.

\subsection{Limitations}

Several limitations define the scope of the present contribution.

First, the study uses a historical U.S. equity and ETF option panel.
Although the ten-ticker design is materially broader than a
single-underlying study, it does not establish robustness across
international equities, equity indices, commodities, foreign exchange,
rates, or cryptocurrency markets. The results should therefore not be
read as evidence that ProtoHedge is already asset-class invariant.

Second, the hedging environment is realistic in important respects---it
uses historical option observations, transaction costs, step-wise
accounting, and hard trading constraints---but it remains a controlled
backtest. It does not fully model bid--ask execution uncertainty,
market impact, funding costs, changing liquidity, margin requirements,
or the operational constraints of a live trading desk. The short-call
liability is also stylized rather than a complete portfolio of actual
client positions.

Third, the current rolling 20-step episode design is well suited to
controlled comparison, but future work should include strictly
time-ordered out-of-sample tests with non-overlapping evaluation
periods. Such tests would provide a stronger assessment of robustness
to non-stationarity and would better isolate performance during
specific stress events.

Fourth, the interpretability analysis is evidence of inspectability,
not external validation of usability. Prototype concentration,
regime-dependent usage, and nearest historical states demonstrate that
the model exposes meaningful internal structure. However, this paper
does not include an evaluation by professional hedgers, portfolio
managers, or risk officers. Whether practitioners find the retrieved
prototype states useful for actual decision support remains an open
question.

Fifth, the study compares ProtoHedge with standard Deep Hedging and
classical delta-style baselines, but not with the full range of recent
deep-hedging architectures. In particular, future work should compare
against deeper or recurrent hedging networks, alternative risk-aware
objectives, and models evaluated under richer dynamics such as
Chiarella--Heston-type environments. Those comparisons are necessary
to locate ProtoHedge more precisely within the broader deep-hedging
literature.

Finally, the present work does not provide a systematic scalability
study. We evaluate several prototype counts and similarity
specifications, but we do not yet fully characterize how computational
cost, prototype count, feature dimensionality, and performance interact
as the problem grows. This is especially relevant for high-dimensional
hedging tasks involving multiple correlated assets, richer option
surfaces, or longer horizons. Approximate nearest-neighbor methods,
more efficient prototype-selection procedures, and trainable prototype
locations are promising directions for addressing this limitation.

\subsection{Path-Dependent and Practical Extensions}

The final Asian-option experiment directly addresses the next empirical
extension proposed in the original ProtoHedge research agenda. Because
an Asian payoff depends on the trajectory of the underlying rather than
only its terminal value, it provides a more demanding test of whether
prototype-based decisions remain useful under path dependence. Once the
full ten-ticker Asian panel is complete, it should be evaluated using
the same performance, bound-occupancy, and interpretability framework
as the European-option results.

Beyond Asian options, barrier options and other path-dependent
liabilities would provide natural stress tests of the framework.
Further empirical work should also identify whether dominant prototypes
correspond to recognizable market events, including crisis periods,
volatility shocks, and rapid drawdowns. The strongest eventual external
validation would combine this quantitative analysis with structured
feedback from professional hedgers who can assess whether prototype
retrievals are economically meaningful and operationally useful.
